scores.evidence: Per-card hot counters are strongly consistent per key (single partition per card, atomic increment in the request path).
scores.rationale: Claims about ISO 8583, Kafka durability settings, Flink checkpointing, HMAC tokenization, Treelite/ONNX in-process serving, TreeSHAP and SR 11-7 are all accurate and precise, including the subtle consistency and skew areas.

scores.evidence: Scoring happens on the issuer or processor side, inside the existing ISO 8583 authorization flow.
scores.rationale: Solves exactly the stated problem (inline real-time scoring), resolves ambiguities with stated assumptions, is credibly buildable in phases, and explicitly defers non-core scope with pull-forward triggers.

scores.evidence: Train on features logged at the moment of the decision ("log-and-wait"). This removes training/serving skew by design.
scores.rationale: Components, contracts and data ownership interlock tightly (decision log is the training set, same feature code for backfill), with consistency, identity and degradation handled uniformly and no contradictions.

scores.evidence: A game day with Redis killed: the scorer degrades and sets the degraded flag, and authorization is unaffected.
scores.rationale: Every phase has checkable exit criteria tied to its specific risks (shadow mode first, replay determinism, feature parity >99.5%, leakage tests, kill-switch drills), and validation continues in production via drift and matured-label monitoring.

scores.evidence: Assumptions (confirm these): The scoring happens on the issuer or processor side... Peak volume is a few thousand transactions per second.
scores.rationale: Assumptions are explicit and flagged for confirmation, every key decision carries a revisit trigger stating what would change it, and numbers are presented as chosen defaults rather than invented facts.

scores.evidence: anomaly checks on labels from each source (defense against insider label poisoning)
scores.rationale: Covers the hard domain failures—scorer outage with fail-open fallback, stale counters, selection bias on declines, reversed chargebacks, adversarial threshold probing, label poisoning, duplicates and late events—each with concrete detection and recovery.

scores.evidence: Kill-switch drill: enforcement is off in under 1 minute with zero auth errors.
scores.rationale: Deploy/rollback, ramps, kill switches, domain-meaningful signals (decline rate per segment, customer-confirmed FP rate), schema migration and drilled incident responses are designed in from day zero; only explicit on-call ownership is unnamed.

scores.evidence: Fewer than about 2 data scientists, or no labeled history. Then buy a vendor platform (Featurespace, Feedzai)
scores.rationale: Build-vs-buy trade-offs, fraud-loss-vs-decline cost reasoning and deferral-based cost controls are solid, but there are no order-of-magnitude run-cost estimates or discussion of how infra cost grows with volume.

scores.evidence: plug it in behind the same scoring API contract, so the choice can be reversed.
scores.rationale: Every decision has a revisit trigger, hard-to-reverse commitments (tokenization keys, schemas, decision-log contract) are front-loaded and validated first, and vendor or serving swaps are isolated behind stable contracts.

scores.evidence: ML model (the flashy part, built last on purpose)
scores.rationale: Starts with the thinnest end-to-end slice (one feature, one rule, shadow mode), defers GNNs, multi-region, commercial feature stores and online learning with explicit triggers, and omits nothing essential.

scores.evidence: Phases (ordered by dependency; within each phase, widest impact first)
scores.rationale: Concrete first steps, dependency-justified ordering, specific implementable decisions (75 ms timeout, CEL rules, Protobuf BACKWARD compat), checkable exit criteria per phase, and explicit adaptation paths if inline scoring or the model disappoints.
